edits.hebrew: מדברי כולן נלמד: רב יהודה, ורבה בר בר חנה, ורב דימי, וריש לקיש, ורבי אבהו.

edits.english: Rav Kahana says: From the statements of all the amora’im who were cited (Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel, Rabbah bar bar Ḥana, Rav Dimi in the name of Rabbi Yoḥanan, and Reish Lakish), we learn that if a forbidden food imparts flavor to the detriment of the mixture, it is permitted. Abaye said to him: Granted, from all of them this conclusion is very well. But how can this be concluded from the statement of Reish Lakish? He says only that the Sages said that if a forbidden food imparts flavor to a permitted food to its detriment, the mixture is permitted, and it implies that he is only citing what others said and he himself does not hold accordingly.

edits.hebrew: מכלל דאיכא למאן דאמר וכו': בתמיה: מדאיצטריך רב כהנא למימר "מדברי כולן נלמד", מכלל דאיכא למאן דפליג.

edits.english: The Gemara returns to discuss the main point of Rav Kahana’s statement, and asks: Does it imply by inference from his words that there is one who says that if a forbidden food imparts flavor to the detriment of the mixture, it is forbidden?

And they answer: Yes, and it is taught in a baraita: Both in a case where the forbidden food imparts flavor to the detriment of the mixture, and in a case where it imparts flavor that enhances the mixture, it is forbidden; this is the statement of Rabbi Meir. Rabbi Shimon says: If it enhances the flavor it is forbidden, but if it causes it detriment it is permitted. This shows that Rabbi Meir holds this opinion.

edits.hebrew: יליף מגיעולי עובדי כוכבים: דרחמנא אסרינהו בכלי מדין, דכתיב: "כל דבר אשר יבא באש" וגו', דמשמע: הואיל ונשתמש עובד כוכבים בכלי חמין, צריך להרתיח כדי שיפלוט גיעול שבלע.
לאו נותן טעם לפגם הוא: בתמיה: דהא פשיטא לן, כל תבשיל שלן לילה אחד, נפגם טעמו ועובר צורתו.

edits.english: And they ask: What is the reasoning of Rabbi Meir? He derives this halakha from the purging of gentiles' vessels, from pots in which gentiles cooked food, for which the Torah required purification for the vessels that Israel plundered from Midian (Numbers 31:22–23). Is it not the case that the purging of gentiles' vessels imparts a detrimental flavor? For the taste of the food in them becomes spoiled over time and only detracts from the food, and nevertheless, the Merciful One prohibited its use. So too, in every case, it is no different, and even a detrimental flavor is forbidden.

And the opinion of the other tanna, Rabbi Shimon, who deems the mixture permitted if the flavor imparted is detrimental, can be explained in accordance with the opinion of Rav Huna, son of Rav Ḥiyya; as Rav Huna, son of Rav Ḥiyya, says: With regard to the vessels of gentiles, the Torah prohibits only a bat yoma pot (a pot that was used for cooking on that very day), which does not yet impart flavor to the detriment of the food cooked in it. Rather, the flavor that it imparts is not considered detrimental. And the opinion of the other tanna, Rabbi Meir, can also be explained in accordance with this statement, as in his opinion, even in the case of a bat yoma pot, it is not possible that it does not detract from the flavor of food that is subsequently cooked in it even slightly.

edits.hebrew: בת יומא: שבישל בה עובד כוכבים היום, דלא נפגם.
ואידך: אי אפשר דלא פגמה פורתא בתבשיל הבא אחריו, ואפ"ה אסר רחמנא.

edits.english: And the other tanna, Rabbi Shimon, who permits a detrimental flavor, what does he respond to this proof? He explains in accordance with the statement of Rav Huna, son of Rav Ḥiyya; as Rav Huna, son of Rav Ḥiyya, says: The Torah prohibits only a bat yoma pot (meaning a pot in which the forbidden food was cooked on that very day), because the flavor it imparts is not detrimental. And the other tanna, Rabbi Meir, what does he say? Even a bat yoma pot, it is not possible that it does not detract slightly from the food since it was cooked, and nevertheless, the Torah prohibited it.

edits.hebrew: ור"ש מאי טעמא דתניא (דברים יד, כא) לא תאכלו כל נבלה לגר אשר בשעריך כל הראויה לגר קרויה נבילה שאין ראויה לגר אינה קרויה נבלה

edits.english: And they ask: And Rabbi Shimon, who holds that imparting a detrimental flavor is permitted, what is his reasoning for his view? As it is taught in a baraita, it is stated: “You shall not eat of any unslaughtered animal carcass; you may give it to the resident alien who is within your gates, that he may eat it” (Deuteronomy 14:21). From here he learns: Anything that is fit for a ger toshav to eat is called an unslaughtered carcass and is forbidden,

The Gemara asks: And what is the reasoning of Rabbi Shimon? It is as it is taught in a baraita that from the verse: “You shall not eat of any unslaughtered animal carcass; you may give it to the resident alien [la’ger] who is within your gates, that he may eat it” (Deuteronomy 14:21), it is derived that with regard to animal carcasses, anything that is fit for a ger toshav to consume is called an unslaughtered carcass and is forbidden, and any carcass that is unfit even for a ger toshav to consume, e.g., one that turned rancid and is unfit for consumption, is not called an unslaughtered carcass with regard to its prohibition.

edits.hebrew: שאינה ראויה לגר: שהסריחה. אלמא מדאפגים, בטל איסורה.

edits.english: That is unfit for a ger toshav, for example, if it spoiled and became rancid and is unfit for consumption — it is not called an unslaughtered carcass with regard to its prohibition.

edits.hebrew: סרוחה מעיקרא: מוכת שחין מחיים, דהואיל ואיפגמא מקודם שבאה לידי נבלה, לא חל שם נבלה עליה. אבל היכא דאיתסר מעיקרא, תו לא פקע איסור משום פגם.

edits.english: And Rabbi Meir, what does he respond to this? He holds: That verse comes to exclude meat that was rancid at the outset, meaning that even in its lifetime it was unfit for consumption due to a repulsive defect, and from the beginning it was not forbidden as a neveilah. But that which was forbidden from the beginning remains forbidden even when its taste becomes detrimental. And Rabbi Shimon, what does he respond to this? Meat that was rancid at the outset does not need exclusion from the verse, because it is considered mere dust, and the name neveilah does not apply to it at all.
